lessons.title: Nouns and Gender
lessons.explanation: Sindhi nouns are masculine or feminine, similar to Hindi and Urdu. Masculine nouns often end in -o (و): ڇوڪرو (chhokro, boy). Feminine nouns often end in -i (ي): ڇوڪري (chhokri, girl).
examples: ڇوڪرو (chhokro) — boy (masculine)
ڇوڪري (chhokri) — girl (feminine)
ڪتاب (kitaab) — book (masculine)
ڪَمِ (kanm) — room (feminine)
lessons.tip: Adjectives and verbs often change their ending to agree with a noun's gender, so learn each noun's gender as you learn its meaning.

quiz.question: What gender is 'ڇوڪري' (chhokri, girl) in Sindhi?

lessons.title: Pronouns and Formality
lessons.explanation: Sindhi pronouns include: مان (maan, I), تون (toon, you — informal singular), توهان (tohan, you — formal/plural), هو (ho, he/she/it), اسين (asin, we).
examples: مان شاگرد آهيان. (maan shagird ahyaan.) — I am a student.
تون منهنجو دوست آهين. (toon manhinjo dost aahin.) — You are my friend. (informal)
توهان ڪٿي رهو ٿا؟ (tohan kithe raho tha?) — Where do you live? (formal)
هو استاد آهي. (ho ustaad ahe.) — He/she is a teacher.
lessons.tip: Use توهان with elders, strangers, and in formal settings; تون with close friends and family your own age or younger.

quiz.question: Which Sindhi pronoun is the more formal/respectful way to say 'you'?

lessons.title: The Verb 'To Be' — آهيان/آهين/آهي
lessons.explanation: The verb 'to be' changes with the subject: آهيان (ahyaan, I am), آهين (ahin, you are — informal), آهي (ahe, he/she/it is), آهيون (ahyoon, we are), آهن (ahn, they are).
examples: مان ٺيڪ آهيان. (maan theek ahyaan.) — I am fine.
تون سٺو آهين. (toon satho ahin.) — You are good. (informal)
هو منهنجو ڀاءُ آهي. (ho manhinjo bhaau ahe.) — He is my brother.
اسين پاڪستاني آهيون. (asin Pakistani ahyoon.) — We are Pakistani.
lessons.tip: The form of 'to be' always matches the subject's person and number — check it carefully when building a sentence.

quiz.question: Which form of 'to be' goes with مان (maan, I)?

lessons.title: Word Order and Postpositions
lessons.explanation: Sindhi is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb), like Hindi, Urdu, and Bangla — the verb comes last. Postpositions follow the noun: ۾ (mein, in), تي (te, on), کان (khaan, from), جو/جي/جا (jo/ji/ja, possessive 'of').
examples: مان ڪتاب پڙهان ٿو. (maan kitaab parhaan tho.) — [I book read] I read a book.
هو اسڪول ۾ آهي. (ho school mein ahe.) — [He school in is] He is in school.
ميز تي ڪتاب آهي. (mez te kitaab ahe.) — [Table on book is] The book is on the table.
ڪراچي کان حيدرآباد (Karachi khaan Hyderabad) — from Karachi to Hyderabad
lessons.tip: As in Hindi/Urdu/Bangla, Sindhi postpositions come AFTER the noun rather than before it.

quiz.question: Where does the verb usually go in a Sindhi sentence?

lessons.title: Present Habitual Tense
lessons.explanation: The present habitual tense uses the verb stem plus ٿو/ٿي (tho/thi, matching gender) plus the 'to be' verb: پڙهان ٿو (parhaan tho, I read — masculine speaker), پڙهان ٿي (parhaan thi, I read — feminine speaker).
examples: مان روز ڪتاب پڙهان ٿو. (maan roz kitaab parhaan tho.) — I read a book every day. (masculine)
تون ڇا ڪرين ٿو؟ (toon chha karen tho?) — What do you do? (informal, masculine)
هوءَ چانھ پيئي ٿي. (hoo chanh peye thi.) — She drinks tea. (feminine)
هو گانو ڳائي ٿو. (ho gaano gaaye tho.) — He sings a song.
lessons.tip: Unlike Bangla or English, the habitual-tense marker in Sindhi (ٿو/ٿي) itself changes with the SPEAKER's gender, not just the subject's person.

quiz.question: What does the ٿو/ٿي marker in the Sindhi present habitual tense agree with?

lessons.title: Postpositions and Case Marking
lessons.explanation: Sindhi postpositions follow the noun. The possessive جو/جي/جا (jo/ji/ja) changes to agree with the gender and number of the thing possessed, much like Hindi का/की/के. کي (khe) marks an indirect or definite direct object ('to/for'), and کان (khaan) means 'from'.
examples: سنڌ جو ماڻهو (Sindh jo maanhu) — a person of Sindh (masculine)
سنڌ جي ٻولي (Sindh ji boli) — the language of Sindh (feminine)
مون کي ڏس. (mun khe des.) — Look at me. (کي marks the object)
ڪراچي کان لاهور (Karachi khaan Lahore) — from Karachi to Lahore
lessons.tip: جو/جي/جا agrees with the possessed noun's gender, exactly like Hindi का/की/के — not with the possessor.

quiz.question: Which form of جو/جي/جا would go with a feminine possessed noun?
What does the postposition کان mean?

lessons.title: Plural Formation
lessons.explanation: Sindhi plurals depend on gender and word ending. Masculine nouns ending in -و (o) usually change to -ا (a) in the plural: ڇوڪرو → ڇوڪرا (boy → boys). Feminine nouns ending in -ي (i) usually change to -يون (iyoon): ڇوڪري → ڇوڪريون (girl → girls).
examples: ڇوڪرو → ڇوڪرا (chhokro → chhokra) — boy → boys
ڇوڪري → ڇوڪريون (chhokri → chhokriyoon) — girl → girls
ڪتاب → ڪتاب (kitaab → kitaab) — book → books (unchanged, ends in consonant)
عورت → عورتون (aurat → auratoon) — woman → women
lessons.tip: As with Hindi, check the noun's gender and final vowel to predict the correct plural pattern.

quiz.question: What is the plural of ڇوڪرو (boy)?
What is the plural of ڇوڪري (girl)?

lessons.title: Question Formation
lessons.explanation: Sindhi yes/no questions are usually formed with rising intonation on a statement, sometimes introduced by ڀلا (bhala, 'well/so'). Wh-questions use question words such as ڇا (chha, what), ڪير (keer, who), ڪٿي (kithe, where), ڪڏهن (kadahn, when), ڇو (chho, why), and ڪيئن (keyen, how).
examples: تون ڇا ڪرين ٿو؟ (toon chha karen tho?) — What are you doing?
تون ڪٿي رهين ٿو؟ (toon kithe rahen tho?) — Where do you live?
هو ڪير آهي؟ (ho keer ahe?) — Who is he?
تون ڪڏهن ايندين؟ (toon kadahn aendin?) — When will you come?
lessons.tip: Question words usually appear in the same position the answer word would occupy, similar to Hindi and Urdu.

quiz.question: Which Sindhi word means 'where'?
Which Sindhi word means 'who'?

lessons.title: Simple Past Tense
lessons.explanation: The simple past in Sindhi also agrees with gender and number: پڙهيو (parhyo, he read), پڙهي (parhi, she read), پڙهيا (parhya, they/plural read).
examples: هن ڪتاب پڙهيو. (hun kitaab parhyo.) — He read the book.
هن ڪتاب پڙهي. (hun kitaab parhi.) — She read the book.
ٻارن ڪتاب پڙهيا. (baaran kitaab parhya.) — The children read the books.
مان اڳي اتي وياس. (maan agi uthe wyaas.) — I went there before.
lessons.tip: Like Hindi and Urdu, Sindhi past-tense verbs agree with the object in certain constructions — pay attention to gender and number endings.

quiz.question: In Sindhi past tense, what commonly changes the verb's ending?

lessons.title: Future Tense
lessons.explanation: The Sindhi future tense adds the suffix -ندو (masculine singular), -ندي (feminine singular), or -نداسين/-ندا (plural) to the verb stem, agreeing with the subject's gender and number: پڙهندو (parhando, he will read), پڙهندي (parhandi, she will read).
examples: هو ڪتاب پڙهندو. (ho kitaab parhando.) — He will read a book.
هوءَ گانو ڳائيندي. (hoo gaano gaayendi.) — She will sing a song.
اسين اسڪول وينداسين. (asin school wendaseen.) — We will go to school.
تون ڇا ڪندين؟ (toon chha kandeen?) — What will you do?
lessons.tip: Future tense endings (-ندو/-ندي/-ندا) must match the subject's gender and number, just like the present habitual marker.

quiz.question: Which suffix marks future tense for a feminine subject in Sindhi?
Complete: هو سڀاڻي ___. (He will come tomorrow.)

lessons.title: Present Continuous Tense
lessons.explanation: Sindhi expresses an action happening right now with پيو/پئي (payo/payi, agreeing with the subject's gender) placed before the verb, combined with the 'to be' auxiliary: هو پيو پڙهي (he is reading right now). This differs from the general present habitual (ٿو/ٿي) used for routine actions.
examples: هو پيو پڙهي. (ho payo parhe.) — He is reading (right now).
هوءَ پئي لکي. (hoo payi likhe.) — She is writing (right now).
ٻار پيا راند ڪن. (baar paya raand kan.) — The children are playing (right now).
مان پيو کاڌو کائان. (maan payo khaadho khaayaan.) — I am eating food (right now).
lessons.tip: Use پيو/پئي for an action happening at this very moment; use the ٿو/ٿي habitual marker for routines and general truths.

quiz.question: What marks an action happening right now in Sindhi?
پيو/پئي changes to agree with what?

lessons.title: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Sindhi comparatives use کان (khaan, 'than') after the noun being compared: هي هن کان وڏو آهي (this is bigger than that). Superlatives use سڀ کان (sabh khaan, 'than all') before the adjective: هي سڀ کان وڏو آهي (this is the biggest).
examples: هي ڪتاب هن کان چڱو آهي. (This book is better than that one.)
احمد سليم کان قد آور آهي. (Ahmed is taller than Saleem.)
هوءَ سڀ کان هوشيار شاگرد آهي. (She is the smartest student.)
هي سڀ کان سستو آهي. (This is the cheapest.)
lessons.tip: کان = 'than' for comparatives; سڀ کان = 'than all' for superlatives, both placed before the adjective.

quiz.question: Which word means 'than' in Sindhi comparisons?
How do you say 'the biggest' in Sindhi?

lessons.title: Reported Speech and Compound Verbs
lessons.explanation: Sindhi reported speech uses ته (te, 'that') after a reporting verb. Sindhi also makes heavy use of compound verbs (a main verb plus a helper verb) to add nuance, such as completion or suddenness.
examples: هن چيو ته هو ٿڪل آهي. (hun cheyo te ho thakal ahe.) — He said that he is tired.
مون کي خبر آهي ته تون سچ چئين ٿو. (mun khe khabar ahe te toon sach chaen tho.) — I know that you are telling the truth.
هو کائي ويو. (ho khaai wyo.) — He ate it up (completely). (compound verb)
هو روئي پيو. (ho roi pyo.) — He suddenly started crying. (compound verb)
lessons.tip: Compound verbs (like کائي ويو 'ate up' vs. simply کاڌائين 'ate') are a hallmark of fluent, natural-sounding Sindhi.

quiz.question: Which word introduces reported speech in Sindhi (like English 'that')?

lessons.title: Passive Voice Constructions
lessons.explanation: The Sindhi passive is formed with the perfective (past participle) form of the main verb plus a form of وڃڻ (wanjan, 'to go'): لکيو ويو (likhyo wyo, 'was written'). If the agent is mentioned, it takes the postposition کان (khaan, 'by').
examples: خط لکيو ويو. (khat likhyo wyo.) — The letter was written.
دروازو کوليو ويو. (darwaazo kholyo wyo.) — The door was opened.
هي ڪم سڀاڻي ڪيو ويندو. (hi kam sabhaani kayo wendo.) — This work will be done tomorrow.
احمد کان اهو ڪم ڪيو ويو. (Ahmed khaan aho kam kayo wyo.) — This work was done by Ahmed.
lessons.tip: Passive = perfective participle + a form of وڃڻ (to go); the agent, if named, takes کان (by), not کي.

quiz.question: Which verb combines with a past participle to form the Sindhi passive?
Which postposition marks the agent in a Sindhi passive sentence?

lessons.title: Honorific and Formal Speech
lessons.explanation: To show respect, Sindhi speakers address one person with the plural pronoun توهان (tohan, 'you' formal) instead of singular تون, and the verb takes the corresponding plural ending: توهان ڪيئن آهيو؟ (How are you?, formal — literally 'are you-plural'). This grammatical plural for respect parallels Hindi and Urdu.
examples: توهان ڪيئن آهيو؟ (tohan keyen ahyo?) — How are you? (formal)
بابا سائين ايندا. (baba saaeen aendaa.) — Father will come. (honorific plural)
ادا صاحب ويٺا آهن. (adaa saahib waitha aahin.) — Brother sir is sitting. (honorific plural)
مهرباني ڪري ويهو. (meharbaani kare weho.) — Please sit down. (formal imperative)
lessons.tip: Grammatically plural verb forms are used to show respect for a single elder or honored person — treat them like Hindi's आप construction.

quiz.question: Which pronoun is used to address one respected person formally in Sindhi?
When using توهان for one person, how does the verb agree?

lessons.title: Conjunctive Participles
lessons.explanation: Sindhi links two actions by the same subject using a conjunctive participle: the first verb's stem takes -ي (i) and means 'having done X,' followed by the main verb: کائي (khai, 'having eaten'), وڃي (wanje, 'having gone'). This lets speakers chain actions without repeating the subject or using a full conjunction.
examples: هو کائي آيو. (ho khai aayo.) — Having eaten, he came. (He ate and then came.)
هوءَ نہائي، تيار ٿي. (hoo nahai, tayaar thi.) — Having bathed, she got ready.
ڪتاب پڙهي، سمهي پيو. (kitaab parhi, samhi pyo.) — Having read the book, he fell asleep.
در کولي، اندر آيو. (dar kholi, andar aayo.) — Having opened the door, he came in.
lessons.tip: The conjunctive participle (stem + ي) is a compact way to say 'after doing X, ...' without a separate word for 'after' or 'and.'

quiz.question: What does the conjunctive participle ending -ي added to a verb stem mean?
In 'هو کائي آيو', what does کائي express?
